blocks.text: Long ago, in the days when King Arthur was young, a woman called Ceridwen lived in the middle of Lake Tegid, in the north of Wales. She knew all kinds of magic. She had a daughter who was the most beautiful girl in the world, and a son who was the ugliest boy in the world. And Ceridwen worried that nobody would ever think much of her son, because he was so ugly, unless he was wiser than anyone else.

So she decided to make him a magic brew from her books of magic: a cauldron of inspiration and knowledge. It had to boil for a year and a day without ever stopping. And at the end of that time, it would give three drops of wonderful magic. Whoever swallowed those three drops would know everything, past and future.

Ceridwen set a boy called Gwion Bach, which means Little Gwion, to stir the cauldron, and a blind old man to keep the fire burning underneath it. "Don't let it stop boiling for a year and a day," she told them. And every day she went out to gather magic herbs to put in it.

Gwion stirred and stirred for nearly a whole year. Then, one day, near the end of the year, while Ceridwen was out gathering herbs, three hot drops jumped out of the cauldron and landed on Gwion's finger. They were so hot that he popped his finger into his mouth.

And at once Gwion knew everything. He knew all that had happened and all that was going to happen. And he knew that as soon as Ceridwen found out, she would be furious. So he ran away as fast as he could.
The cauldron cracked in two, because everything left in it, except those three drops, was poison.
When Ceridwen came back and saw that her whole year's work was lost, she was wild with rage. "It was Gwion Bach who robbed me!" she cried. And she ran after him.

Gwion looked back and saw her coming. So he turned himself into a hare, and ran. But Ceridwen turned herself into a greyhound, and raced after him. He came to a river, and turned himself into a fish, and swam away. But Ceridwen turned herself into an otter, and swam after him. So he leaped out of the water and turned himself into a bird, and flew up into the sky. But Ceridwen turned herself into a hawk, and flew after him. Just as she was about to catch him, he saw a heap of wheat on a barn floor. He dropped down into the wheat, and turned himself into a single grain.
But Ceridwen turned herself into a black hen with a tall crest. She scratched through the wheat with her feet until she found him, and she gobbled him up.

And nine months later, Gwion was born again, as Ceridwen's own baby. She had meant to get rid of him. But he was such a beautiful baby that she could not bear to hurt him. So she wrapped him up in a leather bag and put him into the sea, to drift wherever God would send him.

Now, on the shore near Aberystwyth, a lord called Gwyddno had a fish trap, called a weir, built out into the sea. Every year, on the night before the first of May, a hundred pounds' worth of fish was caught in it. Gwyddno had a son called Elffin, who was the unluckiest young man in the world. So, to see if his luck would change, Gwyddno let Elffin have that year's catch from the weir.
The next morning, Elffin went to look. There were no fish in the weir at all. There was nothing but a leather bag, caught on one of the poles.
"You were never so unlucky as this!" said the weir-keeper. "There's always a hundred pounds' worth of fish, and today there's nothing but this leather bag."
"Who knows?" said Elffin. "There may be a hundred pounds' worth in it."
So they opened the bag. And inside was a baby boy, with a forehead so white and shining that the man cried, "What a radiant brow!" In Welsh, "radiant brow" is "tal iesin".
"Then Taliesin shall be his name," said Elffin. And he picked the baby up and put him gently on the horse behind him, and he rode home very slowly and carefully, so the baby would be comfortable.
And then, to Elffin's astonishment, the baby began to sing.

"Fair Elffin, don't be sad! There was never such good luck in Gwyddno's weir as there was tonight. I may be little, but I have great gifts. Weak and small as I am, in the day of trouble I will be worth more to you than three hundred salmon."
"Did you catch anything?" asked Gwyddno, when Elffin came home.
"Something better than fish," said Elffin. "A poet."
"What good is a poet to you?" said Gwyddno.
"More good than the weir ever was to you," said the baby.
"You can talk, and you so little?" said Gwyddno.
"I can talk better than you can ask questions," said Taliesin.
So Elffin and his wife brought Taliesin up, and from that day on, Elffin's luck changed, and he grew richer every day.

When Taliesin was thirteen, Elffin went to a Christmas feast at the castle of his uncle, the great King Maelgwn. Everyone at the feast was praising the king. "Is there any king in the world so great?" they said. "Who has braver warriors, or faster horses, or a lovelier queen, or wiser poets?" For King Maelgwn had twenty-four poets at his court.

"Nobody can be compared with a king," said Elffin. "But if he wasn't the king, I would say that my wife is as good as any lady in the land, and that I have a poet who is wiser than all the king's poets."

When the king heard this, he was furious, and he threw Elffin into prison, with a silver chain around his feet. And he sent his son to make trouble for Elffin's wife. But Taliesin knew what was coming, and outwitted him.
Then Taliesin said to Elffin's wife, "Don't worry. I will go to the king's court and set my master free."

When Taliesin got to the king's hall, he sat down quietly in a corner, near the door where the poets came in. And when the king's twenty-four poets came marching past, on their way to sing the king's praises, Taliesin pouted out his lips at them, and went "Blerwm, blerwm!" with his finger on his lips.

The poets marched up to the king and bowed. But when they opened their mouths to sing, nothing came out but "Blerwm, blerwm!" They pouted their lips, and played on them with their fingers, and could not say a single word.

"They must be drunk!" said the king. He sent a lord to tell them to behave. But they just went on going "Blerwm, blerwm." At last the king told a servant to hit the chief poet on the head with a broom.
The chief poet fell to his knees. "Great king," he said, "we are not drunk. There is a spirit in this hall, sitting in the corner in the shape of a child, and it has put a spell on us."
So the king had Taliesin brought before him. "Who are you?" he asked. "And where have you come from?"
And Taliesin answered in a song:

"I am Elffin's chief poet, and my first home was the land of the summer stars. I have been with Noah in the ark. I know the names of the stars from north to south. I was little Gwion once, and now I am Taliesin."
The king and all his lords had never heard such a song from someone so young. The king told his poets to answer Taliesin. But they could only go "Blerwm, blerwm."
Then Taliesin sang a riddle:

"What is the strong creature from before the Flood, without flesh, without bone, without head, without feet? It is never older or younger than it was at the beginning. It is in the field, it is in the wood, it is on the sea and on the land. Nobody can see it, but it is the noisiest thing on earth."
And as he sang, a great storm of wind blew up around the castle, so strong that the king and his lords were afraid the walls would fall on their heads. For the answer to the riddle was the wind.
"Bring Elffin here, quickly!" cried the king. And when Elffin was brought before him, Taliesin sang one more song, and the chains fell off Elffin's feet by themselves.

Then Taliesin told Elffin to make a bet with the king that he had a horse faster than any of the king's horses. On the day of the race, the king brought twenty-four of his fastest horses. Taliesin gave Elffin's rider twenty-four sticks of holly, burned black. "Let all the king's horses get ahead of you," he said. "Then, as you catch up with each one, tap it with a holly stick and drop the stick. And wherever your own horse stumbles, throw down your cap."

The rider did exactly as he was told. He caught up with every one of the king's horses, one after another, and tapped each one with a holly stick, and each one fell behind. And he won the race. And where his horse had stumbled, he threw down his cap.
Taliesin brought Elffin to the place where the cap lay, and told him to have the workmen dig there. And they dug, and found a great cauldron full of gold.
"Elffin," said Taliesin, "this is my reward to you, for taking me out of the weir, and for bringing me up."
And there is a pool at that place still, called the Pool of the Cauldron.
A simplified retelling of “Taliesin” in The Mabinogion, translated by Lady Charlotte Guest (1849). The original is listed under Other versions. Guest spells Ceridwen as Caridwen and Elffin as Elphin.
